newsitem.title: UK: Economic minefield awaits UK Labour government.
newsitem.headline: Economic minefield awaits UK Labour government.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party may inherit a fairly healthy economy if it wrests power from the Conservatives in the coming election, but it could quickly face a host of economic pitfalls.

While the country is enjoying steady growth, low inflation and falling unemployment, economists say interest rate rises, tax increases and the vexed problem of a single European currency could all haunt the first years of a Labour government.

"To navigate all these minefields successfully, a future Labour government will need both a good deal of skill and some good fortune," said Andrew Sentance, director of the London Business School's Centre for Economic Forecasting.
Prime Minister John Major must call an election by May 22 and the Labour Party, which is consistently 20 points or more ahead in opinion polls, looks set to win.
Sentance, formerly one of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's independent advisers, says interest rates will have to rise soon after the election to rein in a buoyant domestic economy.

Clarke has so far resisted Bank of England Governor Eddie George's call for base rates to be raised to 6.25 percent from six. But Sentance said consumer spending growth of about four percent this year will force the issue sooner or later.
Interest rate rises are politically sensitive in Britain because two thirds of adults own their own homes, generally purchased with variable rate mortgages.

Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse, sees consumer confidence continuing to increase as house prices rise and millions of people receive "windfall" gains as several mutually owned building societies turn themselves into banks.
Building society pay-outs could total around 20 billion pounds.
"After the election, it will become clear that consumer demand is growing unsustainably fast," Jeffrey said.
"Charterhouse is forecasting a sharp increase in base rates in the second half of the year as the new government struggles to protect the 2.5 percent inflation target."
The Conservative government has a medium-term target of 2.5 percent year-on-year for underlying inflation, a goal that Labour's shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown has adopted.
If that was not bad enough, the political nightmare of tax rises will only be avoided if a lid is kept firmly on public spending, Sentance said.
That could prove difficult despite Brown's pledges to follow Conservative spending plans for the first two years of a Labour government and not to put up income tax rates.

Sentance said public sector workers would push for hefty pay rises after years of enforced wage restraint under the Conservatives and Labour's traditional supporters will expect more spending on education and the health service.
Despite the Labour party's attempt to distance itself from the trade unions -- its traditional allies -- it will find it hard to ignore their claims altogether.

And, as deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine has observed, matching the government's spending plans implies Labour sticking with some Tory policies which it opposes, such as the privatisation of London's underground rail service.
If spending is not curbed, "borrowing is likely to run at an unsustainable level or tax rises will be necessary at some point to pay for higher public spending plans," Sentance said.
Geoffrey Dicks, UK economist at NatWest Markets, offered one solution for Labour -- abolishing tax relief on home loan payments. That could kill two birds with one stone, he said.

"Not only would this provide an extra 2.4 billion pounds of revenues, but it would also mimic a monetary tightening. This would take the steam out of the housing market and, by signalling that base rates will not have to rise, provide a correction to the pound's strength. Labour should go for it."
The strength of the pound, which has jumped 16 percent in the last seven months, is already hurting Britain's exporters by making their goods more expensive abroad.

Perhaps the biggest obstacle facing a Labour government -- and one reason why some Conservatives may not be too concerned about losing the next election -- is the poisoned chalice of a single European currency.
That could prove just as divisive for a Labour government as it has for the Conservative administration in recent years.
A decision will be needed by the end of 1997 as to whether Britain will opt out of the first round of European economic and monetary union (EMU), scheduled for January 1, 1999.
Labour leaders appear to be fundamentally more pro-European than the bulk of the Conservative party but Sentance thinks they will nevertheless probably opt out of the first wave of EMU.
But that would merely postpone the day of reckoning.

"The main economic difficulty is that the UK has no real track record of exchange rate stability against the mark and other countries which are likely to go ahead with EMU," Sentance said. "That creates a very significant risk of serious exchange rate misalignment."
Not all is doom and gloom. Sentance acknowledged that things will be much better for Labour than the last time the party came to power in 1974.
"New Labour would inherit an economy which is no longer held back by the problems of the 'British disease' -- high inflation, industrial unrest and sluggish industrial productivity growth."
Furthermore, a run on the pound, which has traditionally greeted a new Labour government, would not have to be met with higher interest rates because the currency is already too high.
Even so, Labour leader Tony Blair has his eyes wide open.
"Even if we win, there will be no victory dances," he told the Scottish Labour Party this month. "For then, the hard work in serving our country begins in earnest."
